newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican claims PRI is democratic, critics laugh.
newsitem.headline: Mexican claims PRI is democratic, critics laugh.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo claimed on Thursday that his long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) had taken a big step towards greater democracy but critics dubbed the move a sham and said PRI hardliners were gaining ground.
The PRI, which has ruled Mexico for nearly 68 unbroken years, has long been famous for designating key election candidates on orders from the president -- the uncrowned head of the party.
But this year party bosses decided they would choose the PRI's candidate for the key post of Mexico City mayor -- up for election this July for the first time -- by secret ballot.
Expectations were huge, particularly since top PRI officials hinted that the procedure could be a kind of dry run for choosing the next PRI presidential candidate in 1999.

Three mayoral candidates were duly presented. Each ran a mini-campaign before the party faithful and the watching media and on Wednesday night 189 members of the PRI's Mexico City political council met and cast their votes.
Alfredo del Mazo, a former governor of Mexico state linked to party hardliners, flattened his two rivals by 141 votes to 26 to 22. The PRI hierarchy was thrilled.

"Let me tell you that for me, as a Mexican who believes deeply in democracy as a way of life, as a way of thinking, as a way of behaviour, this spectacle which we are seeing is marvellous," Zedillo said at a Rotary Club meeting.

PRI president Humberto Roque Villanueva told reporters after the vote: "This has been an extraordinary exercise in participative democracy of the PRI...the PRI in the capital feels proud of the way they took their decision."
But reporters covering the "vote" and opposition politicians derided the affair as a sham.
They pointed to the fact that up to 10,000 PRI supporters bussed in from the suburbs to cheer the victorious candidate already carried banners hailing Del Mazo long before the vote.
In classic PRI tradition, delegates were also given hints before the vote about who to pick.

Days before the election, veteran union boss Fidel Velasquez -- head of the PRI's powerful old guard labour sector -- attended a Del Mazo campaign meeting but did not do the other two candidates the same favour.
Maria Teresa Gomez Mont, a deputy for the opposition National Action Party (PAN), told Reuters that "of course nobody is going to believe this farce because it was not a democratic process".
Commentators also noted that leading party hardliner Carlos Hank Gonzalez turned up in person to rally support for his protege Del Mazo.
Widely described as one of the PRI's most powerful "dinosaurs", Hank swept into the PRI headquarters to effusive greetings from dozens of party militants.
"We dinosaurs have many friends," he joked before casting his ballot. Reporters asked him whether he had voted for Del Mazo. "Is there anyone else ?" he replied.
